title: Die Gänsehirtin am Brunnen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 179. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Thür, häßlich, wußte). Includes a short rhymed couplet spoken by the old woman about carrying one’s burden.
about: Not to be confused with the Goose-Girl of KHM 89, this long tale wraps a story within a story: a proud young count is made to carry a bundle for a witch-like old goose-herd, and only later does the household turn out to be sheltering a wronged princess in disguise. The narrator keeps stepping back to admit that her own grandmother’s memory of the tale was imperfect, which gives the telling an unusually self-aware, oral texture. A short rhymed couplet from the old woman is the tale’s one piece of inset verse.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein steinaltes Mütterchen, das lebte mit seiner Herde Gänse in einer Einöde zwischen Bergen und hatte da ein kleines Haus.
sentences.l: There was once a stone-old little mother, who lived with her flock of geese in a wilderness among mountains and had there a little house.
sentences.i: There was once an ancient little old woman who lived with her flock of geese in a waste place among the mountains, and had a little house there.
sentences.n: “Mütterchen” is a neuter diminutive, so the German words that follow it are neuter — “seiner Herde”, later “ihm” and “es” — although the person is a woman; English has to say “her”. “steinalt” = stone-old, i.e. ancient. “Herde” here is die Herde, the flock, not der Herd, the hearth.

sentences.t: Die Einöde war von einem großen Wald umgeben, und jeden Morgen nahm die Alte ihre Krücke und wackelte in den Wald.
sentences.l: The wilderness was surrounded by a great forest, and every morning the old woman took her crutch and waddled into the forest.
sentences.i: The waste was ringed by a great wood, and every morning the old woman took her crutch and hobbled off into the wood.
sentences.n: “die Alte” — an adjective used as a noun, “the old woman”; German makes these freely, and this one runs through the whole tale. “wackeln” = to wobble, waddle.

sentences.t: Da war aber das Mütterchen ganz geschäftig, mehr als man ihm bei seinen hohen Jahren zugetraut hatte, sammelte Gras für seine Gänse, brach sich das wilde Obst ab, so weit es mit den Händen reichen konnte, und trug alles auf seinem Rücken heim.
sentences.l: But there the little mother was quite busy, more than one would have credited to her at her high years, gathered grass for her geese, broke off for herself the wild fruit, so far as it could reach with its hands, and carried everything home on her back.
sentences.i: But there the little old woman was busy indeed, more than anyone would have thought her capable of at her great age: she gathered grass for her geese, broke off the wild fruit as far as she could reach with her hands, and carried it all home on her back.
sentences.n: “ihm … es” are neuter because they refer back to “das Mütterchen”. “jemandem etwas zutrauen” = to credit someone with being able to do something. “sich etwas abbrechen” — the dative “sich” says she breaks it off for her own use, and the particle ab- lands at the end. “Obst” here is plain High German fruit.

sentences.t: Man hätte meinen sollen die schwere Last müßte sie zu Boden drücken, aber sie brachte sie immer glücklich nach Haus.
sentences.l: One should have thought the heavy load must press her to the ground, but she always brought it home safely.
sentences.i: You would have thought the heavy load must crush her to the ground, but she always got it safely home.
sentences.n: “Man hätte meinen sollen” = one would have expected; the clause that follows has no “daß” and simply runs on. “müßte” is subjunctive (1857 ß; modern müsste). “nach Haus” = homeward.

sentences.t: Wenn ihr jemand begegnete, so grüßte sie ganz freundlich, „guten Tag, lieber Landsmann, heute ist schönes Wetter.
sentences.l: When someone met her, she greeted quite friendly, “good day, dear countryman, today is beautiful weather.
sentences.i: If anyone met her she greeted him very kindly: “Good day, dear countryman, fine weather today.
sentences.n: “begegnen” takes the dative (“ihr”). The “so” after the “wenn” clause marks the main clause and is best left out of English. “Landsmann” is a warm way of addressing a stranger. Her speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: Ja, ihr wundert euch daß ich das Gras schleppe, aber jeder muß seine Last auf den Rücken nehmen.“
sentences.l: Yes, you wonder yourselves that I drag the grass, but everyone must take his load on his back.
sentences.i: Yes, you are surprised that I am hauling grass about, but everyone must carry his own load on his back.
sentences.n: She addresses the passer-by with the plural “ihr/euch”, the older polite form. “sich wundern” = to be surprised. “daß” is the 1857 spelling of dass.

sentences.t: Doch die Leute begegneten ihr nicht gerne und nahmen lieber einen Umweg,
sentences.l: Yet the people did not gladly meet her and rather took a detour,
sentences.i: But people did not care to meet her, and would rather go round another way,
sentences.n: “lieber” is the comparative of “gern”: they took a detour more gladly, i.e. preferred to. The sentence runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: und wenn ein Vater mit seinem Knaben an ihr vorübergieng, so sprach er leise zu ihm „nimm dich in Acht vor der Alten, die hats faustdick hinter den Ohren: es ist eine Hexe.“
sentences.l: and when a father with his boy went past her, then he spoke softly to him “take yourself in heed of the old woman, she has it fist-thick behind the ears: she is a witch.”
sentences.i: and when a father passed her with his boy, he would say quietly to him: “Beware of that old woman — there is more to her than meets the eye: she is a witch.”
sentences.n: “sich in Acht nehmen vor” = to be on one’s guard against. “es faustdick hinter den Ohren haben” is an idiom — literally to have it fist-thick behind the ears — said of someone sly who is not to be trusted. “vorübergieng” is the 1857 spelling of vorüberging (separable, particle vorüber-).

sentences.t: Eines Morgens gieng ein hübscher junger Mann durch den Wald.
sentences.l: One morning a handsome young man went through the forest.
sentences.i: One morning a handsome young man was walking through the forest.
sentences.n: “Eines Morgens” is a genitive of time: the bare genitive does the work of “on one morning”. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging, and you will meet it on every page.

sentences.t: Die Sonne schien hell, die Vögel sangen, und ein kühles Lüftchen strich durch das Laub, und er war voll Freude und Lust.
sentences.l: The sun shone bright, the birds sang, and a cool little breeze stroked through the foliage, and he was full of joy and delight.
sentences.i: The sun shone bright, the birds were singing, a cool breeze moved through the leaves, and he was full of joy and gladness.
sentences.n: “Lüftchen” — diminutive of Luft, a little breath of air. “streichen” = to brush, sweep, stroke. “Lust” here is delight, high spirits, rather than craving.

sentences.t: Noch war ihm kein Mensch begegnet, als er plötzlich die alte Hexe erblickte, die am Boden auf den Knien saß und Gras mit einer Sichel abschnitt.
sentences.l: Not yet had any person met him, when he suddenly caught sight of the old witch, who sat on the ground on her knees and cut off grass with a sickle.
sentences.i: He had not yet met a soul when suddenly he caught sight of the old witch, kneeling on the ground and cutting grass with a sickle.
sentences.n: German puts “Noch” first and the verb second — the V2 rule — so the subject “kein Mensch” follows the verb. “ihm” is again the dative that “begegnen” takes. “abschneiden” is separable, particle ab-.

sentences.t: Eine ganze Last hatte sie schon in ihr Tragtuch geschoben, und daneben standen zwei Körbe, die mit wilden Birnen und Äpfeln angefüllt waren.
sentences.l: A whole load she had already pushed into her carrying-cloth, and beside it stood two baskets which were filled with wild pears and apples.
sentences.i: She had already stuffed a whole load into her carrying-cloth, and beside it stood two baskets filled with wild pears and apples.
sentences.n: A “Tragtuch” is a cloth in which a load is bundled up to be carried on the back. Fronting the object (“Eine ganze Last”) keeps the verb in second place and pushes the subject behind it.

sentences.t: „Aber, Mütterchen,“ sprach er, „wie kannst du das alles fortschaffen?“
sentences.l: “But, little mother,” he spoke, “how can you carry all that away?”
sentences.i: “But, little mother,” said he, “however can you carry all that off?”
sentences.n: “sprach” is the storyteller’s verb for “said” throughout. He says “du” to the old woman, and she answers with the polite “ihr” — the difference in footing is worth watching. “fortschaffen” = to get something away (separable, particle fort-).

sentences.t: „Ich muß sie tragen, lieber Herr,“ antwortete sie, „reicher Leute Kinder brauchen es nicht.
sentences.l: “I must carry them, dear sir,” answered she, “rich people’s children do not need it.
sentences.i: “I must carry them, dear sir,” she answered; “rich folks’ children are spared it.
sentences.n: “reicher Leute Kinder” — a bare genitive standing in front of its noun, an old and elevated word order; modern German would say “die Kinder reicher Leute”.

sentences.t: Aber beim Bauer heißts
sentences.l: But at the peasant’s it goes
sentences.i: But with the peasant the saying goes:
sentences.n: “heißts” = heißt es, “it is said, the saying goes”; the enclitic -s for “es” is everywhere in these tales. The sentence breaks off here because it runs straight on into the rhyme that follows.

sentences.t:
schau dich nicht um,
dein Buckel ist krumm.“
sentences.l:
look not round you,
your hump is crooked.”
sentences.i:
don’t look round,
your back is bent.”
sentences.n: The German rhymes um / krumm. Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme — the sense is given plainly instead. “schau” here is the imperative of schauen, not the noun die Schau; “sich umschauen” is separable, so the particle um- comes at the end. The couplet is the countryman’s jibe at a back bent by carrying.

sentences.t: „Wollt ihr mir helfen?“ sprach sie, als er bei ihr stehen blieb, „ihr habt noch einen geraden Rücken und junge Beine, es wird euch ein leichtes sein.
sentences.l: “Will you help me?” she spoke, as he stopped standing by her, “you still have a straight back and young legs, it will be an easy thing for you.
sentences.i: “Will you help me?” she said, when he stopped beside her; “you still have a straight back and young legs — it will be nothing to you.
sentences.n: “stehen bleiben” = to stop, stand still. “ein leichtes” is an adjective used as a neuter noun, an easy matter; the dative “euch” says for whom.

sentences.t: Auch ist mein Haus nicht so weit von hier: hinter dem Berge dort steht es auf einer Heide.
sentences.l: Also my house is not so far from here: behind the mountain there it stands on a heath.
sentences.i: And my house is not so far from here: it stands on a heath behind that mountain.
sentences.n: The colon does the work of a “namely” — 1857 punctuation uses it far more freely than English does.

sentences.t: Wie bald seid ihr da hinaufgesprungen.“
sentences.l: How soon you will have sprung up there.”
sentences.i: You will be up there in no time.”
sentences.n: “hinaufgesprungen” — the perfect used for something certain to happen: the German pictures the climb as already done.

sentences.t: Der junge Mann empfand Mitleiden mit der Alten, „zwar ist mein Vater kein Bauer,“ antwortete er, „sondern ein reicher Graf, aber damit ihr seht daß die Bauern nicht allein tragen können, so will ich euer Bündel aufnehmen.“
sentences.l: The young man felt compassion with the old woman, “admittedly my father is no peasant,” he answered, “but a rich count, yet so that you see that the peasants cannot carry alone, I will take up your bundle.”
sentences.i: The young man felt pity for the old woman. “My father is no peasant, it is true,” he answered, “but a rich count; still, so that you may see that peasants are not the only ones who can carry a load, I will take up your bundle.”
sentences.n: Two pairs work at once here: “zwar … aber” concedes and then counters (admittedly …, but still …), while “kein … sondern” corrects a negative (not a peasant, but a count). “damit” + a verb-final clause = so that. “aufnehmen” is separable, particle auf-.

sentences.t: „Wollt ihrs versuchen,“ sprach sie, „so soll mirs lieb sein.
sentences.l: “Will you try it,” she spoke, “then it shall be dear to me.
sentences.i: “If you will try it,” said she, “I shall be glad of it.
sentences.n: A condition without “wenn”: the verb comes first (“Wollt ihrs …”) and carries the sense of “if”. “ihrs” = ihr es; “mirs lieb sein” = to be welcome to me.

sentences.t: Eine Stunde weit werdet ihr freilich gehen müssen, aber was macht euch das aus!
sentences.l: An hour far you will indeed have to go, but what does that matter to you!
sentences.i: You will have a good hour’s walk, to be sure, but what is that to you!
sentences.n: “freilich” concedes: to be sure, admittedly. “was macht euch das aus” = what difference does it make to you.

sentences.t: Dort die Äpfel und Birnen müßt ihr auch tragen.“
sentences.l: There the apples and pears you must carry too.”
sentences.i: Those apples and pears you must carry as well.”
sentences.n: “Dort die Äpfel und Birnen” is set out in front of the sentence, the way a speaker points at something first and then says what about it.

sentences.t: Es kam dem jungen Grafen doch ein wenig bedenklich vor, als er von einer Stunde Wegs hörte, aber die Alte ließ ihn nicht wieder los, packte ihm das Tragtuch auf den Rücken und hieng ihm die beiden Körbe an den Arm.
sentences.l: It seemed to the young count a little questionable, though, when he heard of an hour of way, but the old woman did not let him loose again, packed him the carrying-cloth onto his back and hung the two baskets on his arm.
sentences.i: The young count did think it a little worrying when he heard of an hour’s walk, but the old woman would not let him go; she loaded the carrying-cloth onto his back and hung the two baskets on his arm.
sentences.n: “vorkommen” + dative = to seem to someone (separable, particle vor-). “einer Stunde Wegs” is a genitive: an hour’s worth of road. “packte ihm” — the dative marks the person it is done to. “hieng” = 1857 spelling of hing.

sentences.t: „Seht ihr, es geht ganz leicht,“ sagte sie.
sentences.l: “You see, it goes quite easily,” said she.
sentences.i: “There, you see, it goes quite easily,” said she.
sentences.n: “es geht” — the impersonal “it goes”, i.e. it works, it is manageable.

sentences.t: „Nein es geht nicht leicht“ antwortete der Graf und machte ein schmerzliches Gesicht, „der Bündel drückt ja so schwer, als wären lauter Wackersteine darin, und die Äpfel und Birnen haben ein Gewicht, als wären sie von Blei; ich kann kaum athmen.“
sentences.l: “No it does not go easily” answered the count and made a pained face, “the bundle presses so heavy, as if there were nothing but cobble-stones in it, and the apples and pears have a weight as if they were of lead; I can hardly breathe.”
sentences.i: “No, it does not go easily,” answered the count, pulling a pained face; “the bundle weighs on me as though it were full of cobblestones, and the apples and pears are as heavy as lead — I can hardly breathe.”
sentences.n: “der Bündel” is masculine here; modern German has das Bündel. “als wären” is subjunctive after “as if”. “athmen” is the 1857 spelling of atmen.

sentences.t: Er hatte Lust alles wieder abzulegen, aber die Alte ließ es nicht zu.
sentences.l: He had a mind to lay everything down again, but the old woman did not allow it.
sentences.i: He had a mind to put it all down again, but the old woman would not have it.
sentences.n: “Lust haben” = to have a mind to do something. “zulassen” (separable, particle zu-) = to permit.

sentences.t: „Seht einmal,“ sprach sie spöttisch, „der junge Herr will nicht tragen was ich alte Frau schon so oft fortgeschleppt habe.
sentences.l: “See once,” she spoke mockingly, “the young gentleman will not carry what I, an old woman, have already dragged away so often.
sentences.i: “Just look,” she said mockingly, “the young gentleman will not carry what I, an old woman, have hauled off so often.
sentences.n: “einmal” with an imperative softens it, roughly “just”. “was ich alte Frau” — the noun stands in apposition to “ich”: I, an old woman.

sentences.t: Mit schönen Worten sind sie bei der Hand, aber wenns Ernst wird, so wollen sie sich aus dem Staub machen.
sentences.l: With fine words they are at hand, but when it becomes earnest, then they want to make themselves out of the dust.
sentences.i: They are ready enough with fine words, but when it comes to the point they want to be off.
sentences.n: Two idioms in one line: “bei der Hand sein” = to be ready with something; “sich aus dem Staub machen” = to clear off, make oneself scarce, literally to make oneself out of the dust. “wenns” = wenn es.

sentences.t: Was steht ihr da,“ fuhr sie fort, „und zaudert, hebt die Beine auf.
sentences.l: What are you standing there,” she went on, “and hesitate, lift up your legs.
sentences.i: What are you standing there for,” she went on, “and dawdling — pick up your feet.
sentences.n: “fortfahren” (separable, particle fort-) = to go on speaking. “hebt … auf” is a plural imperative with the particle thrown to the end.

sentences.t: Es nimmt euch niemand den Bündel wieder ab.“
sentences.l: Nobody takes the bundle off you again.”
sentences.i: Nobody is going to take that bundle off you again.”
sentences.n: “abnehmen” + the dative of the person = to take something off someone; “euch” is that dative.

sentences.t: So lange er auf ebener Erde gieng, wars noch auszuhalten, aber als sie an den Berg kamen und steigen mußten, und die Steine hinter seinen Füßen hinabrollten, als wären sie lebendig, da giengs über seine Kräfte.
sentences.l: So long as he went on level ground, it was still to be borne, but when they came to the mountain and had to climb, and the stones rolled down behind his feet as if they were alive, then it went beyond his powers.
sentences.i: As long as he walked on level ground it could still be borne, but when they came to the mountain and had to climb, and the stones went rolling down behind his feet as though they were alive, it was more than his strength could bear.
sentences.n: “wars” = war es, “giengs” = ging es. “noch auszuhalten” — “sein” with “zu” and an infinitive carries a passive sense: still to be endured.

sentences.t: Die Schweißtropfen standen ihm auf der Stirne und liefen ihm bald heiß bald kalt über den Rücken hinab.
sentences.l: The drops of sweat stood on his forehead and ran down his back now hot now cold.
sentences.i: The sweat stood in drops on his forehead and ran down his back, now hot, now cold.
sentences.n: “bald … bald” = now … now, at one moment … at the next. “Stirne” is the older form of Stirn.

sentences.t: „Mütterchen,“ sagte er, „ich kann nicht weiter, ich will ein wenig ruhen.“
sentences.l: “Little mother,” said he, “I can not further, I want to rest a little.”
sentences.i: “Little mother,” said he, “I can go no further, I must rest a little.”
sentences.n: “ich kann nicht weiter” leaves the verb of motion unsaid: German drops “gehen” after a modal when a direction word carries the sense.

sentences.t: „Nichts da,“ antwortete die Alte, „wenn wir angelangt sind, so könnt ihr ausruhen, aber jetzt müßt ihr vorwärts.
sentences.l: “Nothing there,” answered the old woman, “when we have arrived, then you can rest, but now you must forward.
sentences.i: “Nothing of the sort,” answered the old woman; “when we have arrived you may rest, but now you must get on.
sentences.n: “Nichts da” is a brisk refusal — nothing of the kind. Again the verb of motion is left out after the modal: “ihr müßt vorwärts”.

sentences.t: Wer weiß wozu euch das gut ist.“
sentences.l: Who knows what that is good for you.”
sentences.i: Who knows what good it may do you.”
sentences.n: “wozu … gut ist” = what it is good for. “weiß” here is the verb wissen, to know (ich/er weiß) — the same spelling as the adjective “white”, which turns up later in the tale.

sentences.t: „Alte, du wirst unverschämt,“ sagte der Graf und wollte das Tragtuch abwerfen, aber er bemühte sich vergeblich: es hieng so fest an seinem Rücken, als wenn es angewachsen wäre.
sentences.l: “Old woman, you are becoming impudent,” said the count and wanted to throw off the carrying-cloth, but he strove in vain: it hung so fast on his back as if it had grown on.
sentences.i: “Old woman, you are getting insolent,” said the count, and tried to throw off the carrying-cloth; but he struggled in vain — it clung to his back as though it had grown there.
sentences.n: He drops the polite “ihr” and calls her “du”: the courtesy is gone. “sich bemühen” = to exert oneself. “angewachsen wäre” is subjunctive after “als wenn”.

sentences.t: Er drehte und wendete sich, aber er konnte es nicht wieder los werden.
sentences.l: He turned and twisted himself, but he could not get free of it again.
sentences.i: He turned and twisted, but could not get rid of it.
sentences.n: “etwas los werden” = to get rid of something; “los” is the loose, free element in the phrase.

sentences.t: Die Alte lachte dazu und sprang ganz vergnügt auf ihrer Krücke herum.
sentences.l: The old woman laughed at that and sprang quite merrily around on her crutch.
sentences.i: The old woman laughed at this and hopped about quite merrily on her crutch.
sentences.n: “herumspringen” is separable, particle herum-. “dazu” = to that, at that.

sentences.t: „Erzürnt euch nicht, lieber Herr,“ sprach sie, „ihr werdet ja so roth im Gesicht, wie ein Zinshahn.
sentences.l: “Do not anger yourselves, dear sir,” she spoke, “you are becoming so red in the face, like a rent-cock.
sentences.i: “Do not put yourself out, dear sir,” said she; “you are turning as red in the face as a rent-cock.
sentences.n: “sich erzürnen” = to grow angry. A Zinshahn was a cockerel handed over as rent; its red comb makes the comparison for a red face. “roth” is the 1857 spelling of rot.

sentences.t: Tragt euern Bündel mit Geduld, wenn wir zu Hause angelangt sind, so will ich euch schon ein gutes Trinkgeld geben.“
sentences.l: Carry your bundle with patience, when we have arrived at home, then I will give you a good tip.”
sentences.i: Carry your bundle patiently; when we get home I shall give you a handsome reward.”
sentences.n: “euern” = euren. “schon” here is reassuring — never fear, I will. “Trinkgeld” is literally drink-money, a gratuity.

sentences.t: Was wollte er machen? er mußte sich in sein Schicksal fügen und geduldig hinter der Alten herschleichen.
sentences.l: What was he to do? he had to submit himself to his fate and creep patiently along behind the old woman.
sentences.i: What was he to do? He had to bow to his fate and creep along patiently behind the old woman.
sentences.n: “sich in sein Schicksal fügen” = to submit to one’s fate. The 1857 text often begins the next clause with a small letter after a question mark, as here.

sentences.t: Sie schien immer flinker zu werden und ihm seine Last immer schwerer.
sentences.l: She seemed to become ever nimbler and his load to him ever heavier.
sentences.i: She seemed to grow nimbler and nimbler, and his load heavier and heavier.
sentences.n: “immer” with a comparative = ever more, more and more. The second half leaves out the repeated “zu werden”, which is understood from the first.

sentences.t: Auf einmal that sie einen Satz, sprang auf das Tragtuch und setzte sich oben darauf; wie zaundürre sie war, so hatte sie doch mehr Gewicht als die dickste Bauerndirne.
sentences.l: All at once she made a leap, sprang onto the carrying-cloth and set herself on top of it; as fence-dry as she was, she nevertheless had more weight than the stoutest peasant wench.
sentences.i: All at once she gave a bound, sprang onto the carrying-cloth and settled herself on top of it; lean as a fence-rail as she was, she yet weighed more than the stoutest farm girl.
sentences.n: “einen Satz thun” = to make a leap (thun is the 1857 spelling of tun). “zaundürre” — dry as a fence-rail, a homely word for very thin; “wie zaundürre sie war, so …” concedes: thin as she was, still …. “Bauerndirne” is a peasant girl, carrying no insult in 1857 usage.

sentences.t: Dem Jünglinge zitterten die Knie, aber wenn er nicht fortgieng, so schlug ihn die Alte mit einer Gerte und mit Brennesseln auf die Beine.
sentences.l: To the youth the knees trembled, but when he did not go on, then the old woman struck him with a switch and with nettles on the legs.
sentences.i: The young man’s knees trembled, but whenever he stopped the old woman struck him on the legs with a switch and with nettles.
sentences.n: “Dem Jünglinge zitterten die Knie” is a dative of possession — literally “to the youth the knees trembled”, i.e. his knees trembled. German marks whose body part is meant with the dative rather than a possessive. The -e on “Jünglinge” is the old dative ending.

sentences.t: Unter beständigem Ächzen stieg er den Berg hinauf und langte endlich bei dem Haus der Alten an, als er eben niedersinken wollte.
sentences.l: Under constant groaning he climbed the mountain up and arrived at last at the house of the old woman, as he was just about to sink down.
sentences.i: Groaning without a pause he climbed the mountain, and reached the old woman’s house at last, just as he was ready to drop.
sentences.n: “anlangen” (separable, particle an-) = to arrive. “wollte” here is not wanting but being on the point of: he was about to collapse.

sentences.t: Als die Gänse die Alte erblickten, streckten sie die Flügel in die Höhe und die Hälse voraus, liefen ihr entgegen und schrien ihr „wulle, wulle.“
sentences.l: When the geese caught sight of the old woman, they stretched their wings into the height and their necks forward, ran to meet her and cried to her “wulle, wulle.”
sentences.i: When the geese caught sight of the old woman they stretched their wings up and their necks out, ran to meet her and cried after her: “wulle, wulle.”
sentences.n: “wulle, wulle” is the geese’s own cry, and also the call used to bring geese in — it is not the Low German form of “wollte” that the same spelling carries in other tales. “entgegenlaufen” takes the dative (“ihr”).

sentences.t: Hinter der Herde mit einer Ruthe in der Hand gieng eine bejahrte Trulle, stark und groß, aber häßlich wie die Nacht.
sentences.l: Behind the flock, with a rod in her hand, went an aged wench, strong and big, but ugly as the night.
sentences.i: Behind the flock, a switch in her hand, came an elderly creature, strong and big, but ugly as night.
sentences.n: “Herde” here is die Herde, the flock of geese — not der Herd, the hearth, which the same spelling gives in the dative elsewhere. “Trulle” is a coarse word for a woman, something like slattern or wench; the tale is deliberately blunt about her looks.

sentences.t: „Frau Mutter,“ sprach sie zur Alten, „ist euch etwas begegnet? ihr seid so lange ausgeblieben.“
sentences.l: “Mistress Mother,” she spoke to the old woman, “has something befallen you? you have stayed away so long.”
sentences.i: “Mother,” she said to the old woman, “has something happened to you? You have been away so long.”
sentences.n: “Frau Mutter” is a respectful old form of address to one’s mother. “ist euch etwas begegnet” — begegnen with the dative again: has anything befallen you. “ausbleiben” is separable, particle aus-.

sentences.t: „Bewahre, mein Töchterchen,“ erwiderte sie, „mir ist nichts Böses begegnet, im Gegentheil der liebe Herr da hat mir meine Last getragen;
sentences.l: “Heaven forbid, my little daughter,” she replied, “nothing bad has befallen me, on the contrary the dear gentleman there has carried my load for me;
sentences.i: “Nothing of the sort, my little daughter,” she replied; “no harm has come to me — on the contrary, this good gentleman here has carried my load for me;
sentences.n: “Bewahre!” is an exclamation of denial, short for “Gott bewahre”, God forbid. “im Gegentheil” is the 1857 spelling of im Gegenteil.

sentences.t: denk dir, als ich müde war, hat er mich selbst noch auf den Rücken genommen.
sentences.l: just think to yourself, when I was tired, he even took me himself onto his back.
sentences.i: just imagine — when I grew tired he took me on his back as well.
sentences.n: “denk dir” is the imperative of denken with a dative reflexive: just imagine. It is plain High German here, not the Low German form the same spelling carries in the Low German tales. Every word of her account is a lie.

sentences.t: Der Weg ist uns auch gar nicht lang geworden, wir sind lustig gewesen und haben immer Spaß miteinander gemacht.“
sentences.l: The way did not become long to us either, we were merry and always made fun with one another.”
sentences.i: The road did not seem long to us either — we were merry and joked together the whole way.”
sentences.n: “uns” is another dative of the person concerned: the way did not grow long for us. “Spaß machen” = to joke, make merry.

sentences.t: Endlich rutschte die Alte herab, nahm dem jungen Mann den Bündel vom Rücken und die Körbe vom Arm, sah ihn ganz freundlich an und sprach „nun setzt euch auf die Bank vor die Thüre und ruht euch aus.
sentences.l: At last the old woman slid down, took the young man the bundle from his back and the baskets from his arm, looked at him quite kindly and spoke “now sit down on the bench before the door and rest yourselves.
sentences.i: At last the old woman slid down, took the bundle from the young man’s back and the baskets from his arm, looked at him very kindly and said: “Now sit down on the bench before the door and rest.
sentences.n: “nahm dem jungen Mann den Bündel” — the dative again marks the person something is taken from. “ansehen” is separable, particle an-. “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Tür.

sentences.t: Ihr habt euern Lohn redlich verdient, der soll auch nicht ausbleiben.“
sentences.l: You have honestly earned your wage, and it shall not fail to come.”
sentences.i: You have fairly earned your wage, and it shall not be withheld.”
sentences.n: “ausbleiben” = to fail to appear, not materialise. “redlich” = honestly, fairly.

sentences.t: Dann sprach sie zu der Gänsehirtin „geh du ins Haus hinein, mein Töchterchen, es schickt sich nicht daß du mit einem jungen Herrn allein bist, man muß nicht Öl ins Feuer gießen;
sentences.l: Then she spoke to the goose-herdess “go you into the house, my little daughter, it is not fitting that you are alone with a young gentleman, one must not pour oil into the fire;
sentences.i: Then she said to the goose-girl: “Go into the house, my little daughter; it is not seemly for you to be alone with a young gentleman — there is no need to pour oil on the fire;
sentences.n: “Gänsehirtin” is the feminine of Hirt, the one who tends the flock — the tale’s title word. “sich schicken” = to be fitting, seemly. “Öl ins Feuer gießen” is the same picture as the English pouring oil on the flames.

sentences.t: er könnte sich in dich verlieben.“
sentences.l: he could fall in love with you.”
sentences.i: he might fall in love with you.”
sentences.n: “sich verlieben in” takes the accusative. The old woman is being wry: the reader has just been told what the daughter looks like by day.

sentences.t: Der Graf wußte nicht ob er weinen oder lachen sollte.
sentences.l: The count did not know whether he should weep or laugh.
sentences.i: The count did not know whether to laugh or cry.
sentences.n: “wußte” — the 1857 ß in the past of wissen (modern wusste).

sentences.t: „Solch ein Schätzchen,“ dachte er, „und wenn es dreißig Jahre jünger wäre, könnte doch mein Herz nicht rühren.“
sentences.l: “Such a little treasure,” thought he, “and if it were thirty years younger, it still could not move my heart.”
sentences.i: “Such a sweetheart,” he thought, “and even if she were thirty years younger, she could not stir my heart.”
sentences.n: “Schätzchen” — little treasure, the ordinary word for a sweetheart, said here in mockery. The pronoun is neuter (“es”) because Schätzchen is a neuter diminutive; English has to choose “she”.

sentences.t: Indessen hätschelte und streichelte die Alte ihre Gänse wie Kinder und gieng dann mit ihrer Tochter in das Haus.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the old woman petted and stroked her geese like children and then went with her daughter into the house.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the old woman fondled and stroked her geese like children, and then went into the house with her daughter.
sentences.n: “Indessen” = meanwhile. “hätscheln” = to fondle, make a pet of — the same word used of spoiling a child.

sentences.t: Der Jüngling streckte sich auf die Bank unter einem wilden Apfelbaum.
sentences.l: The youth stretched himself on the bench under a wild apple tree.
sentences.i: The young man stretched himself out on the bench beneath a wild apple tree.
sentences.n: “sich strecken” — the reflexive makes it stretch oneself out at full length.

sentences.t: Die Luft war lau und mild: rings umher breitete sich eine grüne Wiese aus, die mit Himmelsschlüsseln, wildem Thymian und tausend andern Blumen übersät war:
sentences.l: The air was mild and soft: round about spread itself out a green meadow which was strewn over with cowslips, wild thyme and a thousand other flowers:
sentences.i: The air was warm and mild; all around spread a green meadow sown thick with cowslips, wild thyme and a thousand other flowers;
sentences.n: “lau” = lukewarm, balmy. “Himmelsschlüssel” — heaven’s-keys, the German name for the cowslip. “sich ausbreiten” is separable, particle aus-. The colons chain the picture together where English wants semicolons.

sentences.t: mitten durch rauschte ein klarer Bach, auf dem die Sonne glitzerte:
sentences.l: right through it rushed a clear brook, on which the sun glittered:
sentences.i: through the middle of it ran a clear brook with the sun glittering on it;
sentences.n: “mitten durch” = right through the middle. “rauschen” is the sound word — to rush, to murmur.

sentences.t: und die weißen Gänse giengen auf und ab spazieren oder pudelten sich im Wasser.
sentences.l: and the white geese went walking up and down or dabbled themselves in the water.
sentences.i: and the white geese walked up and down, or splashed about in the water.
sentences.n: “spazieren gehen” = to go for a walk. “sich pudeln” = to duck and splash oneself in water, an old word that survives in Pudel, the water dog.

sentences.t: „Es ist recht lieblich hier,“ sagte er, „aber ich bin so müde, daß ich die Augen nicht aufbehalten mag: ich will ein wenig schlafen.
sentences.l: “It is really lovely here,” said he, “but I am so tired that I cannot keep my eyes open: I want to sleep a little.
sentences.i: “It is very pleasant here,” said he, “but I am so tired I cannot keep my eyes open — I will sleep a little.
sentences.n: “aufbehalten” = to keep open; after the modal it stays whole. “mag” here is can, care to, rather than the modern “like”.

sentences.t: Wenn nur kein Windstoß kommt und bläst mir meine Beine vom Leib weg, denn sie sind mürb wie Zunder.“
sentences.l: If only no gust of wind comes and blows my legs away from my body, for they are crumbly as tinder.”
sentences.i: If only no gust of wind comes and blows my legs off my body — they are as brittle as tinder.”
sentences.n: “mürb” (modern mürbe) = crumbly, brittle. “Zunder” is tinder, the dry stuff that takes a spark. His joke is that the climb has worn his legs to nothing.

sentences.t: Als er ein Weilchen geschlafen hatte, kam die Alte, und schüttelte ihn wach.
sentences.l: When he had slept a little while, the old woman came and shook him awake.
sentences.n: “Weilchen” is the diminutive of Weile, a little while. “wach” stands as a predicate adjective: shook him awake.

sentences.t: „Steh auf,“ sagte sie, „hier kannst du nicht bleiben.
sentences.l: “Stand up,” said she, “here you cannot stay.
sentences.i: “Get up,” said she, “you cannot stay here.
sentences.n: “aufstehen” is separable, particle auf-, so the imperative splits it: “steh auf”. She says “du” to him now that his service is over.

sentences.t: Freilich habe ich dirs sauer genug gemacht, aber das Leben hats doch nicht gekostet.
sentences.l: Certainly I have made it sour enough for you, but it has not cost your life.
sentences.i: I have made things hard enough for you, to be sure, but it has not cost you your life.
sentences.n: “es jemandem sauer machen” = to make it hard going for someone. “dirs” = dir es, “hats” = hat es. German says only “das Leben”, the life; whose life is meant is understood from the “dir” just before.

sentences.t: Jetzt will ich dir deinen Lohn geben, Geld und Gut brauchst du nicht, da hast du etwas anderes.“
sentences.l: Now I will give you your wage, money and goods you do not need, here you have something else.”
sentences.i: Now I will give you your wage. Money and goods you have no need of — here is something else.”
sentences.n: “Geld und Gut” is a set pair, money and property. The object is put first, which keeps the verb in second place.

sentences.t: Damit steckte sie ihm ein Büchslein in die Hand, das aus einem einzigen Smaragd geschnitten war.
sentences.l: With that she put a little box into his hand which was cut out of a single emerald.
sentences.i: With that she put into his hand a little box cut from a single emerald.
sentences.n: “Büchslein” — the diminutive of die Büchse, a small lidded box. “stecken” = to put, slip, stick.

sentences.t: „Bewahrs wohl,“ setzte sie hinzu, „es wird dir Glück bringen.“
sentences.l: “Keep it well,” she added, “it will bring you luck.”
sentences.i: “Keep it safe,” she added; “it will bring you good fortune.”
sentences.n: “Bewahrs” = bewahre es, an imperative with the enclitic -s. “hinzusetzen” (separable, particle hinzu-) = to add in speech.

sentences.t: Der Graf sprang auf, und da er fühlte daß er ganz frisch und wieder bei Kräften war, so dankte er der Alten für ihr Geschenk und machte sich auf den Weg ohne nach dem schönen Töchterchen auch nur einmal umzublicken.
sentences.l: The count sprang up, and since he felt that he was quite fresh and again in strength, he thanked the old woman for her gift and made himself on the way without looking back at the beautiful little daughter even once.
sentences.i: The count sprang up, and feeling quite fresh and his strength returned, he thanked the old woman for her gift and set off without so much as one backward glance at the fair daughter.
sentences.n: “bei Kräften sein” = to be in one’s strength. “sich auf den Weg machen” = to set out. “ohne … umzublicken” — “ohne zu” with an infinitive = without doing something, and the “zu” slips in between particle and verb: um-zu-blicken. The daughter he will not look at is the one he ends by loving.

sentences.t: Als er schon eine Strecke weg war, hörte er noch aus der Ferne das lustige Geschrei der Gänse.
sentences.l: When he was already a stretch away, he still heard from the distance the merry crying of the geese.
sentences.i: When he was already some way off he could still hear the merry clamour of the geese in the distance.
sentences.n: “eine Strecke” = a stretch, some distance. “Geschrei” is a collective in Ge-, the continuous shrieking of many voices.

sentences.t: Der Graf mußte drei Tage in der Wildnis herum irren, ehe er sich heraus finden konnte.
sentences.l: The count had to stray about three days in the wilderness before he could find his way out.
sentences.i: The count had to wander three days in the wilds before he could find his way out.
sentences.n: “herum irren” is written as two words in 1857 (modern herumirren). “sich heraus finden” = to find one’s way out.

sentences.t: Da kam er in eine große Stadt, und weil ihn niemand kannte, ward er in das königliche Schloß geführt, wo der König und die Königin auf dem Thron saßen.
sentences.l: Then he came into a great city, and because nobody knew him, he was led into the royal castle, where the king and the queen sat on the throne.
sentences.i: Then he came to a great city, and because nobody knew him he was taken to the royal castle, where the king and queen sat upon their throne.
sentences.n: “ward” is the old past of werden (modern wurde); here it forms the passive — he was led.

sentences.t: Der Graf ließ sich auf ein Knie nieder, zog das smaragdene Gefäß aus der Tasche und legte es der Königin zu Füßen.
sentences.l: The count let himself down on one knee, drew the emerald vessel out of his pocket and laid it at the queen’s feet.
sentences.i: The count went down on one knee, drew the emerald vessel from his pocket and laid it at the queen’s feet.
sentences.n: “sich niederlassen” is separable, particle nieder-. “smaragden” = made of emerald; “Gefäß” is any vessel or container.

sentences.t: Sie hieß ihn aufstehen und er mußte ihr das Büchslein hinauf reichen.
sentences.l: She bade him stand up and he had to reach the little box up to her.
sentences.i: She bade him rise, and he had to hand the little box up to her.
sentences.n: “hieß” is from heißen in its older sense “to bid, to command” — sie hieß ihn aufstehen, she bade him rise. The same form elsewhere means “was called”; here it does not.

sentences.t: Kaum aber hatte sie es geöffnet und hinein geblickt, so fiel sie wie todt zur Erde.
sentences.l: But hardly had she opened it and looked inside, when she fell as if dead to the earth.
sentences.i: But scarcely had she opened it and looked inside than she fell to the ground as if dead.
sentences.n: “Kaum …, so …” = hardly … when. “todt” is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: Der Graf ward von den Dienern des Königs festgehalten und sollte in das Gefängnis geführt werden,
sentences.l: The count was held fast by the servants of the king and was to be led into the prison,
sentences.i: The count was seized by the king’s servants and was to be taken to prison,
sentences.n: “ward … festgehalten” — a passive with the old past of werden. “sollte geführt werden” = was to be taken.

sentences.t: da schlug die Königin die Augen auf und rief sie sollten ihn frei lassen, und jedermann sollte hinaus gehen, sie wollte insgeheim mit ihm reden.
sentences.l: then the queen struck her eyes open and called they should let him free, and everyone should go out, she wanted to speak with him in secret.
sentences.i: when the queen opened her eyes and called out that they were to let him go, and that everyone should leave — she wished to speak with him in private.
sentences.n: “die Augen aufschlagen” = to open one’s eyes. The reported speech follows “rief” with no “daß” at all, the clauses simply running on. “insgeheim” = secretly.

sentences.t: Als die Königin allein war, fieng sie bitterlich an zu weinen und sprach „was hilft mir Glanz und Ehre, die mich umgeben, jeden Morgen erwache ich mit Sorgen und Kummer.
sentences.l: When the queen was alone, she began bitterly to weep and spoke “what helps me splendour and honour, which surround me, every morning I awake with sorrows and grief.
sentences.i: When the queen was alone she began to weep bitterly, and said: “What good to me are the splendour and honour that surround me? Every morning I wake with sorrow and care.
sentences.n: “fieng … an” — anfangen, separable, particle an-; “fieng” is the 1857 spelling of fing. “was hilft mir …” = what does it help me, i.e. what use is it to me.

sentences.t: Ich habe drei Töchter gehabt, davon war die jüngste so schön, daß sie alle Welt für ein Wunder hielt.
sentences.l: I have had three daughters, of whom the youngest was so beautiful that all the world held her for a wonder.
sentences.i: I had three daughters, and the youngest of them was so beautiful that all the world thought her a marvel.
sentences.n: “davon” = of them, of that. “halten für” = to take for, to consider.

sentences.t: Sie war so weiß wie Schnee, so roth wie Apfelblüthe, und ihr Haar so glänzend wie Sonnenstrahlen.
sentences.l: She was as white as snow, as red as apple blossom, and her hair as shining as sunbeams.
sentences.i: She was as white as snow, as red as apple-blossom, and her hair as bright as sunbeams.
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the adjective, white; earlier in the tale the same spelling was the verb wissen, to know (“wer weiß”), and it returns in that sense a few lines on. The two fall together in German. “Apfelblüthe” is the 1857 spelling of Apfelblüte.

sentences.t: Wenn sie weinte so fielen nicht Thränen aus ihren Augen, sondern lauter Perlen und Edelsteine.
sentences.l: When she wept then there fell not tears out of her eyes, but nothing but pearls and precious stones.
sentences.i: When she wept, it was not tears that fell from her eyes but pearls and jewels, and nothing else.
sentences.n: “lauter” = nothing but, sheer. “nicht … sondern” corrects a negative, where “aber” would only add to it. “Thränen” is the 1857 spelling of Tränen.

sentences.t: Als sie fünfzehn Jahr alt war, da ließ der König alle drei Schwestern vor seinen Thron kommen.
sentences.l: When she was fifteen years old, then the king let all three sisters come before his throne.
sentences.i: When she was fifteen years old the king had all three sisters brought before his throne.
sentences.n: “Jahr” stays singular after a numeral in this old counting usage. “ließ … kommen” — lassen with an infinitive = to have someone come.

sentences.t: Da hättet ihr sehen sollen was die Leute für Augen machten, als die jüngste eintrat, es war als wenn die Sonne aufgieng.
sentences.l: There you should have seen what eyes the people made, when the youngest entered, it was as if the sun rose.
sentences.i: You should have seen how the people stared when the youngest came in — it was as though the sun were rising.
sentences.n: Behind “was die Leute für Augen machten” lies “große Augen machen”, to make big eyes, i.e. to stare. “was für” = what sort of. “als wenn” = as if; here it keeps the plain indicative “aufgieng” rather than the subjunctive one might expect. “aufgieng” = aufging, from aufgehen (separable, particle auf-).

sentences.t: Der König sprach „meine Töchter, ich weiß nicht wann mein letzter Tag kommt, ich will heute bestimmen was eine jede nach meinem Tode erhalten soll.
sentences.l: The king spoke “my daughters, I do not know when my last day comes, I will determine today what each one shall receive after my death.
sentences.i: The king said: “My daughters, I do not know when my last day will come; I will settle today what each of you is to have after my death.
sentences.n: “eine jede” = each one (feminine). “nach meinem Tode” keeps the old dative -e on Tod.

sentences.t: Ihr alle habt mich lieb, aber welche mich von euch am liebsten hat, die soll das beste haben.“
sentences.l: You all have me dear, but whichever of you has me dearest, she shall have the best.”
sentences.i: You all love me, but whichever of you loves me most shall have the best.”
sentences.n: “lieb haben” = to hold dear, to love; “am liebsten haben” is its superlative, to love most of all. The whole tale turns on a father asking for love to be measured.

sentences.t: Jede sagte sie hätte ihn am liebsten.
sentences.l: Each said she had him dearest.
sentences.i: Each said that she loved him most.
sentences.n: “hätte” is subjunctive, the mark of reported speech: this is her claim, not the storyteller’s.

sentences.t: „Könnt ihr mirs nicht ausdrücken,“ erwiederte der König, „wie lieb ihr mich habt? daran werde ichs sehen wie ihrs meint.“
sentences.l: “Can you not express it to me,” replied the king, “how dear you have me? by that I shall see how you mean it.”
sentences.i: “Can you not put it into words for me,” the king answered, “how dearly you love me? By that I shall see what you mean.”
sentences.n: “ausdrücken” is separable, particle aus-. “erwiederte” is the 1857 spelling of erwiderte. “ichs”, “ihrs” = ich es, ihr es.

sentences.t: Die älteste sprach „ich habe den Vater so lieb wie den süßesten Zucker.“
sentences.l: The eldest spoke “I have the father as dear as the sweetest sugar.”
sentences.i: The eldest said: “I love my father as dearly as the sweetest sugar.”
sentences.n: German says “den Vater”, the father, where English wants “my father”: the definite article does the work of the possessive with family members.

sentences.t: Die zweite „ich habe den Vater so lieb wie mein schönstes Kleid.“
sentences.l: The second “I have the father as dear as my most beautiful dress.”
sentences.i: The second: “I love my father as dearly as my finest dress.”
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is left out altogether — the pattern of the first answer carries over into the second.

sentences.t: Die jüngste aber schwieg.
sentences.l: The youngest, however, was silent.
sentences.i: But the youngest was silent.
sentences.n: “schweigen” is a verb in its own right, to be silent; German does not need to say “keep silence”.

sentences.t: Da fragte der Vater „und du, mein liebstes Kind, wie lieb hast du mich?“
sentences.l: Then the father asked “and you, my dearest child, how dear do you have me?”
sentences.i: Then the father asked: “And you, my dearest child, how dearly do you love me?”
sentences.n: He puts the question in the same measuring form — “wie lieb”, how dear — that the two elder daughters have already answered.

sentences.t: „Ich weiß es nicht,“ antwortete sie, „und kann meine Liebe mit nichts vergleichen.“
sentences.l: “I do not know it,” answered she, “and cannot compare my love with anything.”
sentences.i: “I do not know,” she answered, “and I can compare my love with nothing.”
sentences.n: German keeps the object “es” where English simply drops it. “mit nichts vergleichen” = to compare with nothing.

sentences.t: Aber der Vater bestand darauf, sie müßte etwas nennen.
sentences.l: But the father insisted on it that she must name something.
sentences.i: But the father insisted that she must name something.
sentences.n: “bestehen auf” = to insist on; “darauf” points forward to the clause that follows. “müßte” is again the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: Da sagte sie endlich „die beste Speise schmeckt mir nicht ohne Salz, darum habe ich den Vater so lieb wie Salz.“
sentences.l: Then she said at last “the best food does not taste to me without salt, therefore I have the father as dear as salt.”
sentences.i: Then at last she said: “The finest dish has no taste for me without salt, and so I love my father as I love salt.”
sentences.n: “schmecken” takes the dative: food tastes good to someone. She measures love by the thing nothing can do without; her father hears only that she has compared him to something cheap, and the whole tale hangs on that misunderstanding.

sentences.t: Als der König das hörte, gerieth er in Zorn und sprach „wenn du mich so liebst als Salz, so soll deine Liebe auch mit Salz belohnt werden.“
sentences.l: When the king heard that, he fell into wrath and spoke “if you love me thus, as salt, then your love shall also be rewarded with salt.”
sentences.i: When the king heard that he flew into a rage and said: “If you love me like salt, then your love shall be repaid with salt.”
sentences.n: “in Zorn gerathen” = to fall into a rage (gerieth is the 1857 spelling of geriet). “so … als” is the older form of “so … wie”, as … as. His sentence turns her own word into her punishment.

sentences.t: Da theilte er das Reich zwischen den beiden ältesten, der jüngsten aber ließ er einen Sack mit Salz auf den Rücken binden, und zwei Knechte mußten sie hinaus in den wilden Wald führen.
sentences.l: Then he divided the kingdom between the two eldest, but to the youngest he had a sack of salt bound onto her back, and two farmhands had to lead her out into the wild forest.
sentences.i: Then he divided the kingdom between the two elder ones; but the youngest he had a sack of salt tied to her back, and two servants had to lead her out into the wild forest.
sentences.n: “ließ … binden” — lassen with an infinitive again, to have something done. “theilte” is the 1857 spelling of teilte. The sack of salt is the sentence carried out to the letter.

sentences.t: „Wir haben alle für sie gefleht und gebeten,“ sagte die Königin, „aber der Zorn des Königs war nicht zu erweichen.
sentences.l: “We have all pleaded and begged for her,” said the queen, “but the wrath of the king was not to be softened.
sentences.i: “We all pleaded and begged for her,” said the queen, “but the king’s anger was not to be softened.
sentences.n: “gebeten” here is the past participle of bitten in its plain sense, to beg, entreat — not the older sense “invited” that the same form carries in other tales. “war nicht zu erweichen” — “sein” with “zu” and an infinitive gives a passive of possibility: could not be softened.

sentences.t: Wie hat sie geweint, als sie uns verlassen mußte! der ganze Weg ist mit Perlen besät worden, die ihr aus den Augen geflossen sind.
sentences.l: How she wept, when she had to leave us! the whole way has been strewn with pearls which flowed to her out of the eyes.
sentences.i: How she wept when she had to leave us! The whole road was strewn with pearls that fell from her eyes.
sentences.n: “Wie hat sie geweint” — an exclamation in the perfect, the ordinary spoken past. “die ihr aus den Augen geflossen sind” — the dative “ihr” names the person: literally “which flowed to her out of the eyes”, i.e. from her eyes.

sentences.t: Den König hat bald hernach seine große Härte gereut und hat das arme Kind in dem ganzen Wald suchen lassen, aber niemand konnte sie finden.
sentences.l: Soon afterwards his great hardness has repented the king, and [he] has had the poor child searched for in the whole forest, but nobody could find her.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards the king repented of his great harshness, and had the poor child searched for through the whole forest, but nobody could find her.
sentences.n: “Den König hat … gereut” — with reuen the person who feels the regret stands in the accusative (“den König”) and the thing regretted is the subject (“seine große Härte”), so English has to turn the sentence round, as the idiomatic line does. The second clause has no subject of its own — German simply carries the king over from the accusative — so “[he]” is supplied in square brackets in the literal line. “hernach” = afterwards.

sentences.t: Wenn ich denke daß sie die wilden Thiere gefressen haben, so weiß ich mich vor Traurigkeit nicht zu fassen;
sentences.l: When I think that the wild beasts have devoured her, then I do not know how to hold myself for sadness;
sentences.i: When I think that the wild beasts have devoured her, I cannot contain myself for grief;
sentences.n: “sich nicht zu fassen wissen” = not to know how to compose oneself. “vor Traurigkeit” — “vor” with a feeling gives the cause: for, with. “Thiere” is the 1857 spelling of Tiere.

sentences.t: manchmal tröste ich mich mit der Hoffnung, sie sei noch am Leben und habe sich in einer Höhle versteckt oder bei mitleidigen Menschen Schutz gefunden.
sentences.l: sometimes I comfort myself with the hope she is still alive and has hidden herself in a cave or found shelter with compassionate people.
sentences.i: sometimes I comfort myself with the hope that she is still living, and has hidden in a cave or found shelter with kindly people.
sentences.n: “sie sei … habe …” is subjunctive I, the form for reported speech and thought; it keeps the hope at arm’s length, as something said rather than known.

sentences.t: Aber stellt euch vor, als ich euer Smaragdbüchslein aufmachte, so lag eine Perle darin, gerade der Art, wie sie meiner Tochter aus den Augen geflossen sind, und da könnt ihr euch vorstellen wie mir der Anblick das Herz bewegt hat.
sentences.l: But imagine to yourselves, when I opened your little emerald box, there lay a pearl in it, exactly of the kind as those which have flowed to my daughter out of the eyes, and then you can imagine to yourselves how the sight has moved my heart.
sentences.i: But imagine — when I opened your little emerald box there lay a pearl in it, exactly of the kind that used to fall from my daughter’s eyes; and you can think for yourself how the sight moved my heart.
sentences.n: “sich etwas vorstellen” = to imagine (separable, particle vor-); it comes twice here, as an imperative and then as a statement. “der Art” is a genitive of description: of that kind.

sentences.t: Ihr sollt mir sagen wie ihr zu der Perle gekommen seid.“
sentences.l: You shall tell me how you came to the pearl.”
sentences.i: You must tell me how you came by the pearl.”
sentences.n: “sollen” here is not obligation but urgent request — you are to tell me.

sentences.t: Der Graf erzählte ihr daß er sie von der Alten im Walde erhalten hätte, die ihm nicht geheuer vorgekommen wäre, und eine Hexe sein müßte; von ihrem Kinde aber hätte er nichts gehört und gesehen.
sentences.l: The count told her that he had received it from the old woman in the forest, who had not seemed canny to him and must be a witch; of her child, however, he had heard and seen nothing.
sentences.i: The count told her that he had had it from the old woman in the forest, who had struck him as uncanny and must surely be a witch; but of her child he had heard and seen nothing.
sentences.n: The whole report stands in the subjunctive — “hätte”, “wäre”, “müßte” — which is how German marks speech reported at second hand. English cannot copy that, so the “that” clause has to carry it. “nicht geheuer” = uncanny, not right.

sentences.t: Der König und die Königin faßten den Entschluß die Alte aufzusuchen; sie dachten, wo die Perle gewesen wäre, da müßten sie auch Nachricht von ihrer Tochter finden.
sentences.l: The king and the queen seized the resolve to seek out the old woman; they thought, where the pearl had been, there they must also find news of their daughter.
sentences.i: The king and queen resolved to seek out the old woman; they thought that where the pearl had been, there they must also find news of their daughter.
sentences.n: “einen Entschluß fassen” = to take a decision. “aufsuchen” is separable, particle auf-. “müßten” is again the subjunctive of reported thought.

sentences.t: Die Alte saß draußen in der Einöde bei ihrem Spinnrad und spann.
sentences.l: The old woman sat outside in the wilderness at her spinning-wheel and spun.
sentences.i: The old woman sat out in the waste at her spinning-wheel, spinning.
sentences.n: “spann” is the past of spinnen — not to be confused with “Span”, the wood splinter that appears in the very next line.

sentences.t: Es war schon dunkel geworden, und ein Span, der unten am Herd brannte, gab ein sparsames Licht.
sentences.l: It had already become dark, and a splinter which burned below at the hearth gave a sparing light.
sentences.i: It had grown dark already, and a chip of wood burning at the hearth gave a scant light.
sentences.n: A “Span” is a thin splinter of resinous wood — the poor household’s lamp, burnt at the hearth for light. “sparsam” = sparing, scant.

sentences.t: Auf einmal wards draußen laut, die Gänse kamen heim von der Weide und ließen ihr heiseres Gekreisch hören.
sentences.l: All at once it became loud outside, the geese came home from the pasture and let their hoarse screeching be heard.
sentences.i: All at once there was a noise outside: the geese came home from the pasture and set up their hoarse screeching.
sentences.n: “wards” = ward es, it became. “hören lassen” = to let be heard, to utter. “Gekreisch” is a collective in Ge-: continuous screeching.

sentences.t: Bald hernach trat auch die Tochter herein.
sentences.l: Soon afterwards the daughter too stepped in.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards the daughter came in too.
sentences.n: “hereintreten” = to step in (separable, particle herein-); the particle marks the direction, in towards the speaker.

sentences.t: Aber die Alte dankte ihr kaum und schüttelte nur ein wenig mit dem Kopf.
sentences.l: But the old woman hardly thanked her and shook only a little with her head.
sentences.i: But the old woman scarcely thanked her, and only shook her head a little.
sentences.n: German says “mit dem Kopf schütteln”, to shake with the head, where English shakes the head itself.

sentences.t: Die Tochter setzte sich zu ihr nieder, nahm ihr Spinnrad und drehte den Faden so flink wie ein junges Mädchen.
sentences.l: The daughter set herself down beside her, took her spinning-wheel and turned the thread as nimbly as a young girl.
sentences.i: The daughter sat down beside her, took the spinning-wheel and turned the thread as nimbly as a young girl.
sentences.n: “sich niedersetzen” is separable: the particle nieder- lands at the end. Her nimble hands give her away before the tale says anything.

sentences.t: So saßen beide zwei Stunden, und sprachen kein Wort mit einander.
sentences.l: So both sat two hours, and spoke no word with one another.
sentences.i: So the two of them sat for two hours and did not speak a word to each other.
sentences.n: “mit einander” is written as two words in 1857 (modern miteinander).

sentences.t: Endlich raschelte etwas am Fenster und zwei feurige Augen glotzten herein.
sentences.l: At last something rustled at the window and two fiery eyes goggled in.
sentences.i: At last something rustled at the window, and two fiery eyes glared in.
sentences.n: “glotzen” = to stare, to goggle. “herein” marks the direction: in towards the watcher.

sentences.t: Es war eine alte Nachteule, die dreimal uhu schrie.
sentences.l: It was an old night-owl which cried uhu three times.
sentences.i: It was an old night-owl, and it cried uhu three times.
sentences.n: “uhu” is the owl’s call; the German name of the eagle owl, der Uhu, is taken straight from the sound. Three cries are the tale’s signal that the hour has come.

sentences.t: Die Alte schaute nur ein wenig in die Höhe, dann sprach sie „jetzt ists Zeit, Töchterchen, daß du hinaus gehst, thu deine Arbeit.“
sentences.l: The old woman looked only a little into the height, then she spoke “now it is time, little daughter, that you go out, do your work.”
sentences.i: The old woman only looked up a little, and then said: “Now it is time, little daughter, for you to go out — do your work.”
sentences.n: “in die Höhe” = upward. “ists” = ist es. “thu” is the imperative of thun, the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Sie stand auf und gieng hinaus.
sentences.l: She stood up and went out.
sentences.n: Two separable verbs in a row: “aufstehen” gives “stand auf”, “hinausgehen” gives “gieng hinaus”.

sentences.t: „Wo ist sie denn hingegangen?“ über die Wiesen immer weiter bis in das Thal.
sentences.l: “Where has she then gone?” over the meadows ever further until into the valley.
sentences.i: “And where did she go?” — over the meadows, further and further, down into the valley.
sentences.n: The storyteller breaks in with her own question and then answers it without a verb; the 1857 text prints the question inside quotation marks, as if a listener had asked it. “Thal” is the 1857 spelling of Tal.

sentences.t: Endlich kam sie zu einem Brunnen, bei dem drei alte Eichbäume standen.
sentences.l: At last she came to a well by which three old oak trees stood.
sentences.i: At last she came to a well with three old oak trees standing by it.
sentences.n: “Brunnen” is a well or spring — the well of the tale’s title, Die Gänsehirtin am Brunnen. “Eichbäume” = oak trees (Eiche + Baum).

sentences.t: Der Mond war indessen rund und groß über dem Berg aufgestiegen, und es war so hell, daß man eine Stecknadel hätte finden können.
sentences.l: The moon had meanwhile risen round and big over the mountain, and it was so bright that one could have found a pin.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the moon had risen round and large above the mountain, and it was so bright you could have found a pin.
sentences.n: “indessen” = meanwhile. “aufsteigen” is separable, particle auf-. The pin is the household measure of a very fine light.

sentences.t: Sie zog eine Haut ab, die auf ihrem Gesicht lag, bückte sich dann zu dem Brunnen und fieng an sich zu waschen.
sentences.l: She drew off a skin which lay on her face, bent herself then to the well and began to wash herself.
sentences.i: She drew off a skin that lay over her face, then bent down to the well and began to wash.
sentences.n: “abziehen” is separable, particle ab-; “fieng an” is anfangen. The skin is a mask worn over the face — the tale’s disguise, and its central object.

sentences.t: Als sie fertig war, tauchte sie auch die Haut in das Wasser, und legte sie dann auf die Wiese, damit sie wieder im Mondschein bleichen und trocknen sollte.
sentences.l: When she was ready, she dipped the skin too into the water, and laid it then on the meadow, so that it should bleach and dry again in the moonshine.
sentences.i: When she had finished she dipped the skin in the water too, and then laid it on the meadow, so that it might bleach and dry again in the moonlight.
sentences.n: “fertig sein” = to be finished. “damit” + a verb-final clause = so that. Linen was bleached by being left out in sun or moonlight; the skin is treated exactly like washing.

sentences.t: Aber wie war das Mädchen verwandelt!
sentences.l: But how was the girl transformed!
sentences.i: But how changed the girl was!
sentences.n: “Wie” with the verb straight after it makes an exclamation, not a question: how the girl was transformed. The storyteller steps out of the scene here and speaks to her listeners directly, as she does again in the next line.

sentences.t: So was habt ihr nie gesehen!
sentences.l: Such a thing you have never seen!
sentences.i: You have never seen the like!
sentences.n: “So was” = so etwas, such a thing — the short spoken form. She addresses her listeners as “ihr”, keeping them in the room with her.

sentences.t: Als der graue Zopf abfiel, da quollen die goldenen Haare wie Sonnenstrahlen hervor und breiteten sich, als wärs ein Mantel, über ihre ganze Gestalt.
sentences.l: When the grey plait fell off, then the golden hairs welled forth like sunbeams and spread themselves, as if it were a mantle, over her whole figure.
sentences.i: When the grey plait fell away, the golden hair welled out like sunbeams and spread, as though it were a cloak, over her whole figure.
sentences.n: “abfallen” and “hervorquellen” are both separable. “wärs” = wäre es, subjunctive after “als”. German has “die Haare” in the plural where English has one word, hair.

sentences.t: Nur die Augen blitzten heraus so glänzend wie die Sterne am Himmel, und die Wangen schimmerten in sanfter Röthe wie die Äpfelblüthe.
sentences.l: Only the eyes flashed out so shining as the stars in the sky, and the cheeks shimmered in soft redness like the apple blossom.
sentences.i: Only her eyes flashed out, as bright as the stars in the sky, and her cheeks glowed a soft red like apple-blossom.
sentences.n: German uses the plain article for parts of the body where English says “her”. “Röthe” = Röte; the 1857 text prints “Äpfelblüthe” here and “Apfelblüthe” earlier — both are apple blossom.

sentences.t: Aber das schöne Mädchen war traurig.
sentences.l: But the beautiful girl was sad.
sentences.n: “Mädchen” is neuter, so the pronouns that follow are neuter — “es”, “seinen”, “ihm” — where English must say “she” and “her”.

sentences.t: Es setzte sich nieder und weinte bitterlich.
sentences.l: It set itself down and wept bitterly.
sentences.i: She sat down and wept bitterly.
sentences.n: The neuter “es” is grammatical gender following “Mädchen”, not coldness on the storyteller’s part; the literal line keeps it visible.

sentences.t: Eine Thräne nach der andern drang aus seinen Augen und rollte zwischen den langen Haaren auf den Boden.
sentences.l: One tear after the other pressed out of its eyes and rolled between the long hair onto the ground.
sentences.i: One tear after another forced its way from her eyes and rolled down through her long hair to the ground.
sentences.n: “dringen” = to press, to force one’s way. These are the pearls of the queen’s story, though the tale does not yet say so.

sentences.t: So saß es da und wäre lange sitzen geblieben, wenn es nicht in den Ästen des nahestehenden Baumes geknittert und gerauscht hätte.
sentences.l: So it sat there and would have remained sitting long, if it had not creaked and rustled in the branches of the tree standing near.
sentences.i: So she sat there, and would have sat long, had there not been a creaking and rustling in the branches of the tree near by.
sentences.n: “wäre … sitzen geblieben” is the subjunctive of an unreal condition. In the “wenn” clause “es” is impersonal: there was a creaking. “knittern” = to creak, crackle.

sentences.t: Sie sprang auf wie ein Reh, das den Schuß des Jägers vernimmt.
sentences.l: She sprang up like a roe deer which hears the shot of the huntsman.
sentences.i: She sprang up like a deer that catches the sound of the hunter’s shot.
sentences.n: The pronoun switches here from the neuter “es” of “Mädchen” to “sie”, the person — the tale slips out of grammar into sympathy. “vernehmen” = to perceive, to hear.

sentences.t: Der Mond ward gerade von einer schwarzen Wolke bedeckt, und im Augenblick war das Mädchen wieder in die alte Haut geschlüpft, und verschwand wie ein Licht, das der Wind ausbläst.
sentences.l: The moon was just then covered by a black cloud, and in the moment the girl had slipped again into the old skin, and vanished like a light which the wind blows out.
sentences.i: Just then the moon was covered by a black cloud, and in an instant the girl had slipped back into the old skin and vanished like a candle the wind blows out.
sentences.n: “ward … bedeckt” — passive with the old past of werden. “ausblasen” is separable, particle aus-.

sentences.t: Zitternd wie ein Espenlaub lief sie zu dem Haus zurück.
sentences.l: Trembling like an aspen leaf she ran back to the house.
sentences.i: Trembling like a leaf she ran back to the house.
sentences.n: “zittern wie ein Espenlaub” — the German says aspen foliage where English says a leaf; the aspen’s leaves shake in the least wind.

sentences.t: Die Alte stand vor der Thüre, und das Mädchen wollte ihr erzählen was ihm begegnet war, aber die Alte lachte freundlich und sagte „ich weiß schon alles.“
sentences.l: The old woman stood before the door, and the girl wanted to tell her what had happened to it, but the old woman laughed friendly and said “I know everything already.”
sentences.i: The old woman was standing at the door, and the girl wanted to tell her what had happened to her, but the old woman laughed kindly and said: “I know it all already.”
sentences.n: “ihm” is neuter, referring to “das Mädchen”. “weiß” here is the verb wissen, to know — the same spelling as the adjective “white” used of the daughter earlier.

sentences.t: Sie führte es in die Stube und zündete einen neuen Span an.
sentences.l: She led it into the parlour and lit a new splinter.
sentences.i: She led her into the room and lit a fresh splinter of wood.
sentences.n: “anzünden” is separable: “zündete … an”. The Span from the hearth serves again as the household lamp.

sentences.t: Aber sie setzte sich nicht wieder zu dem Spinnrad, sondern sie holte einen Besen, und fieng an zu kehren und zu scheuern.
sentences.l: But she did not set herself again to the spinning-wheel, but rather she fetched a broom, and began to sweep and to scour.
sentences.i: But she did not sit down at the spinning-wheel again; instead she fetched a broom and began to sweep and scour.
sentences.n: “sondern” corrects the preceding negative — not that, but this. “scheuern” is the verb to scour, to scrub.

sentences.t: „Es muß alles rein und sauber sein“ sagte sie zu dem Mädchen.
sentences.l: “Everything must be clean and tidy” said she to the girl.
sentences.i: “Everything must be clean and neat,” she said to the girl.
sentences.n: “rein und sauber” is a set pair, clean and spotless. The 1857 text prints no comma before “sagte”.

sentences.t: „Aber, Mutter,“ sprach das Mädchen, „warum fangt ihr in so später Stunde die Arbeit an? was habt ihr vor?“
sentences.l: “But, mother,” spoke the girl, “why do you begin the work at so late an hour? what have you before?”
sentences.i: “But, mother,” said the girl, “why do you begin work at such a late hour? What is it you intend?”
sentences.n: “anfangen” splits around the sentence: “fangt ihr … an”. “vorhaben” (separable, particle vor-) = to have in mind, to intend. The girl says the polite “ihr”; the old woman answers with “du”.

sentences.t: „Weißt du denn welche Stunde es ist?“ fragte die Alte.
sentences.l: “Do you know then which hour it is?” asked the old woman.
sentences.i: “Do you know what hour it is?” asked the old woman.
sentences.n: “denn” inside a question is a flavour word: it colours the question rather than translating, roughly “tell me”.

sentences.t: „Noch nicht Mitternacht,“ antwortete das Mädchen, „aber schon elf Uhr vorbei?“
sentences.l: “Not yet midnight,” answered the girl, “but already past eleven o’clock?”
sentences.i: “Not midnight yet,” answered the girl, “but past eleven already?”
sentences.n: The question mark at the end is the 1857 text’s own — the girl’s answer trails up into uncertainty rather than settling.

sentences.t: „Denkst du nicht daran,“ fuhr die Alte fort, „daß du heute vor drei Jahren zu mir gekommen bist?
sentences.l: “Do you not think of it,” the old woman went on, “that today three years ago you came to me?
sentences.i: “Have you forgotten,” the old woman went on, “that three years ago today you came to me?
sentences.n: “an etwas denken” = to think of something, and “daran” points ahead to the “daß” clause. “heute vor drei Jahren” = three years ago today.

sentences.t: Deine Zeit ist aus, wir können nicht länger beisammen bleiben.“
sentences.l: Your time is out, we cannot stay together longer.”
sentences.i: Your time is up; we cannot stay together any longer.”
sentences.n: “aus sein” = to be at an end. The three years’ service is the term nobody has mentioned until now.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen erschrack und sagte „ach, liebe Mutter, wollt ihr mich verstoßen? wo soll ich hin? ich habe keine Freunde und keine Heimath, wohin ich mich wenden kann.
sentences.l: The girl was startled and said “ah, dear mother, will you cast me out? where am I to go? I have no friends and no home whither I can turn.
sentences.i: The girl was frightened and said: “Ah, dear mother, will you turn me out? Where am I to go? I have no friends and no home to turn to.
sentences.n: “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of erschrak. “wo soll ich hin” drops the verb of motion after the modal, as German readily does. “Heimath” = Heimat.

sentences.t: Ich habe alles gethan was ihr verlangt habt, und ihr seid immer zufrieden mit mir gewesen: schickt mich nicht fort.“
sentences.l: I have done everything you demanded, and you have always been content with me: do not send me away.”
sentences.i: I have done everything you asked, and you have always been satisfied with me — do not send me away.”
sentences.n: “gethan” = getan. “fortschicken” is separable, so the imperative splits it: “schickt mich nicht fort”.

sentences.t: Die Alte wollte dem Mädchen nicht sagen was ihm bevorstand.
sentences.l: The old woman did not want to tell the girl what stood before it.
sentences.i: The old woman did not want to tell the girl what lay ahead of her.
sentences.n: “bevorstehen” + dative = to lie ahead for someone (separable, particle bevor-). “ihm” is neuter for “Mädchen” again.

sentences.t: „Meines Bleibens ist nicht länger hier,“ sprach sie zu ihm, „wenn ich aber ausziehe, muß Haus und Stube sauber sein: darum halt mich nicht auf in meiner Arbeit.
sentences.l: “There is no longer a staying of mine here,” she spoke to it, “but when I move out, house and parlour must be clean: therefore do not hold me up in my work.
sentences.i: “My time here is at an end,” she said to her, “but when I move out, house and room must be clean — so do not hold me up in my work.
sentences.n: “Meines Bleibens ist nicht länger hier” is an old genitive turn of phrase — the noun “das Bleiben”, staying, stands in the genitive as the thing of which there is no more, so the sense is that her stay here is over. “aufhalten” is separable: “halt … auf”.

sentences.t: Deinetwegen sei ohne Sorgen, du sollst ein Dach finden, unter dem du wohnen kannst, und mit dem Lohn, den ich dir geben will, wirst du auch zufrieden sein.“
sentences.l: On your account be without cares, you shall find a roof under which you can live, and with the wage which I will give you, you will also be content.”
sentences.i: On your own account have no fear: you shall find a roof to live under, and you will be well satisfied with the wage I mean to give you.”
sentences.n: “deinetwegen” = on your account, for your sake — one of a family of forms (meinetwegen, seinetwegen). “sei ohne Sorgen” is the imperative of sein.

sentences.t: „Aber sagt mir nur was ist vor?“ fragte das Mädchen weiter.
sentences.l: “But just tell me what is before?” asked the girl further.
sentences.i: “But do tell me what is coming?” the girl asked again.
sentences.n: “was ist vor” shows only the particle of the vorhaben / bevorstehen family — a compressed spoken form, roughly “what is afoot”. The 1857 text is elliptical here; nothing has been left out of the source.

sentences.t: „Ich sage dir nochmals störe mich nicht in meiner Arbeit.
sentences.l: “I tell you once more do not disturb me in my work.
sentences.i: “I tell you again: do not disturb me at my work.
sentences.n: “nochmals” = once again. The command follows “ich sage dir” with no “that” and no comma — German lets the two clauses run straight together.

sentences.t: Rede kein Wort weiter, geh in deine Kammer, nimm die Haut vom Gesicht und zieh das seidene Kleid an, das du trugst als du zu mir kamst, und dann harre in deiner Kammer, bis ich dich rufe.“
sentences.l: Speak not a word further, go into your chamber, take the skin from your face and put on the silken dress which you wore when you came to me, and then wait in your chamber until I call you.”
sentences.i: Say not another word: go into your chamber, take the skin from your face and put on the silk dress you wore when you came to me, and then wait in your chamber until I call you.”
sentences.n: “anziehen” is separable: “zieh … an”. “trugst” and “kamst” are the 2nd person singular past of tragen and kommen. “harren” = to wait, to abide — an elevated old word for warten.

sentences.t: Aber ich muß wieder von dem König und der Königin erzählen, die mit dem Grafen ausgezogen waren und die Alte in der Einöde aufsuchen wollten.
sentences.l: But I must tell again of the king and the queen, who had set out with the count and wanted to seek out the old woman in the wilderness.
sentences.i: But I must go back to the king and queen, who had set out with the count and meant to seek the old woman in the wilderness.
sentences.n: The storyteller speaks in her own person (“ich muß”) to turn the tale back to another thread — the same voice that will close the tale. “ausziehen” is separable, particle aus-.

sentences.t: Der Graf war Nachts in dem Walde von ihnen abgekommen, und mußte allein weiter gehen.
sentences.l: The count had at night become separated from them in the forest, and had to go on alone.
sentences.i: In the night the count had become separated from them in the forest and had to go on alone.
sentences.n: “Nachts” is an adverbial genitive, by night. “abkommen von” = to lose touch with, to get away from.

sentences.t: Am andern Tag kam es ihm vor, als befände er sich auf dem rechten Weg.
