sentences.l: On the next day it seemed to him as if he found himself on the right way.
sentences.i: The next day it seemed to him that he was on the right road.
sentences.n: “befände” is subjunctive after “als (ob)” — the appearance is not vouched for. “vorkommen” + dative again = to seem to someone.

sentences.t: Er gieng immer fort, bis die Dunkelheit einbrach, da stieg er auf einen Baum und wollte da übernachten, denn er war besorgt er möchte sich verirren.
sentences.l: He went ever on until the darkness broke in, then he climbed up a tree and wanted to spend the night there, for he was anxious he might lose his way.
sentences.i: He walked on and on until darkness fell; then he climbed a tree, meaning to pass the night there, for he was afraid of losing his way.
sentences.n: “einbrechen” = to set in, to fall (of night). “möchte” is subjunctive: he feared he might. “sich verirren” = to go astray.

sentences.t: Als der Mond die Gegend erhellte, so erblickte er eine Gestalt, die den Berg herabwandelte.
sentences.l: When the moon lit up the region, he caught sight of a figure which walked down the mountain.
sentences.i: When the moon lit up the country round, he caught sight of a figure coming down the mountain.
sentences.n: The “so” that follows the “als” clause simply marks the main clause and is best left out of English. “herabwandeln” = to walk down, a deliberately stately word.

sentences.t: Sie hatte keine Ruthe in der Hand, aber er konnte doch sehen daß es die Gänsehirtin war, die er früher bei dem Haus der Alten gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: She had no rod in her hand, but he could nevertheless see that it was the goose-herdess whom he had earlier seen at the house of the old woman.
sentences.i: She had no switch in her hand, but he could see all the same that it was the goose-girl he had seen before at the old woman’s house.
sentences.n: “doch” inside a clause = all the same, nevertheless. The missing switch is what makes him look twice.

sentences.t: „Oho!“ rief er, „da kommt sie, und habe ich erst die eine Hexe, so soll mir die andere auch nicht entgehen.“
sentences.l: “Oho!” he cried, “there she comes, and once I have the one witch, then the other shall not escape me either.”
sentences.i: “Oho!” he cried. “There she comes; and once I have the one witch, the other shall not escape me either.”
sentences.n: “erst” here = once, first of all. “entgehen” takes the dative (“mir”). He still takes both women for witches, which is the tale’s standing joke against him.

sentences.t: Wie erstaunte er aber, als sie zu dem Brunnen trat, die Haut ablegte und sich wusch, als die goldenen Haare über sie herabfielen, und sie so schön war, wie er noch niemand auf der Welt gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: But how astonished he was, when she stepped to the well, laid off the skin and washed herself, when the golden hairs fell down over her, and she was so beautiful as he had seen nobody in the world.
sentences.i: But how astonished he was when she came to the well, laid aside the skin and washed, and the golden hair fell down over her, and she was more beautiful than anyone he had ever seen in the world.
sentences.n: “Wie erstaunte er” — an exclamation with the verb first. “ablegen” is separable, particle ab-. The comparison is stretched over a negative: as beautiful as no one he had ever seen.

sentences.t: Kaum daß er zu athmen wagte, aber er streckte den Hals zwischen dem Laub so weit vor, als er nur konnte, und schaute sie mit unverwandten Blicken an.
sentences.l: Hardly that he dared to breathe, but he stretched his neck forward between the foliage as far as he only could, and looked at her with unmoving glances.
sentences.i: He hardly dared to breathe, but he stretched his neck forward through the leaves as far as ever he could, and gazed at her without taking his eyes away.
sentences.n: “Kaum daß …” = scarcely did he …. “nur” strengthens “so weit als er konnte”: as far as he possibly could. “unverwandt” = unmoving, fixed, of a gaze. “vorstrecken” and “ansehen” are both separable, and their particles are stacked at the end of the sentence.

sentences.t: Ob er sich zu weit überbog, oder was sonst Schuld war, plötzlich krachte der Ast,
sentences.l: Whether he bent himself over too far, or what else was to blame, suddenly the branch cracked,
sentences.i: Whether he leaned out too far, or whether something else was at fault, all at once the branch cracked,
sentences.n: “Ob … oder …” with no main verb sets two guesses side by side: the storyteller does not claim to know which. “sich überbiegen” = to bend oneself over too far.

sentences.t: und in demselben Augenblick schlüpfte das Mädchen in die Haut, sprang wie ein Reh davon, und da der Mond sich zugleich bedeckte, so war sie seinen Blicken entzogen.
sentences.l: and in the same moment the girl slipped into the skin, sprang away like a roe deer, and since the moon covered itself at the same time, she was withdrawn from his glances.
sentences.i: and in that same instant the girl slipped into the skin and sprang away like a deer; and as the moon covered itself at that moment, she was lost to his sight.
sentences.n: “entziehen” = to withdraw, to take away from, and it takes the dative (“seinen Blicken”). German has the moon covering itself, where English would say a cloud covered it.

sentences.t: Kaum war sie verschwunden, so stieg der Graf von dem Baum herab und eilte ihr mit behenden Schritten nach.
sentences.l: Hardly had she vanished, when the count climbed down from the tree and hurried after her with nimble steps.
sentences.i: Scarcely had she vanished before the count climbed down from the tree and hurried after her with quick steps.
sentences.n: “Kaum …, so …” = hardly … when. “nacheilen” is separable, particle nach-, and it takes the dative (“ihr”). “behende” (modern behände) = nimble, quick.

sentences.t: Er war noch nicht lange gegangen, so sah er in der Dämmerung zwei Gestalten über die Wiese wandeln.
sentences.l: He had not been going long, when he saw in the twilight two figures walking over the meadow.
sentences.i: He had not gone far before he saw two figures walking across the meadow in the half-light.
sentences.n: “Dämmerung” is the half-light of dawn or dusk; here it is the hour before morning. “wandeln” is an elevated word for walking.

sentences.t: Es war der König und die Königin, die hatten aus der Ferne das Licht in dem Häuschen der Alten erblickt und waren drauf zu gegangen.
sentences.l: It was the king and the queen, they had caught sight of the light in the little house of the old woman from the distance and had gone towards it.
sentences.i: It was the king and queen: they had seen the light in the old woman’s little house from far off and had made towards it.
sentences.n: “die hatten” — a demonstrative used as a pronoun, very common in spoken German. “drauf zu gegangen” = darauf zu gegangen, gone towards it.

sentences.t: Der Graf erzählte ihnen was er für Wunderdinge bei dem Brunnen gesehen hätte, und sie zweifelten nicht daß das ihre verlorene Tochter gewesen wäre.
sentences.l: The count told them what wonder-things he had seen at the well, and they did not doubt that that had been their lost daughter.
sentences.i: The count told them what marvels he had seen at the well, and they did not doubt that it had been their lost daughter.
sentences.n: “Wunderdinge” — wonder-things, marvels. “hätte” and “wäre” are again the subjunctives that mark a report at second hand.

sentences.t: Voll Freude giengen sie weiter und kamen bald bei dem Häuschen an: die Gänse saßen rings herum, hatten den Kopf in die Flügel gesteckt und schliefen, und keine regte sich nicht.
sentences.l: Full of joy they went further and soon arrived at the little house: the geese sat round about, had put their heads in their wings and slept, and not one stirred itself.
sentences.i: Full of joy they went on, and soon came to the little house. The geese were sitting all around, their heads tucked into their wings, asleep, and not one of them stirred.
sentences.n: “keine regte sich nicht” is a double negative — ordinary in older and spoken German for emphasis, and it does not cancel itself: not one stirred. “rings herum” = round about.

sentences.t: Sie schauten zum Fenster hinein, da saß die Alte ganz still und spann, nickte mit dem Kopf und sah sich nicht um.
sentences.l: They looked in at the window, there sat the old woman quite still and spun, nodded with her head and did not look round.
sentences.i: They looked in at the window: there sat the old woman, quite still, spinning; she nodded her head and did not look round.
sentences.n: “sich umsehen” is separable, particle um-. “spann” is once more the past of spinnen, not the splinter Span.

sentences.t: Es war ganz sauber in der Stube, als wenn da die kleinen Nebelmännlein wohnten, die keinen Staub auf den Füßen tragen.
sentences.l: It was quite clean in the parlour, as if the little mist-men lived there who carry no dust on their feet.
sentences.i: The room was perfectly clean, as though the little mist-men lived there, who carry no dust on their feet.
sentences.n: “Nebelmännlein” — little mist-men, house spirits of German folk belief who leave no trace behind them. “als wenn” takes the subjunctive.

sentences.t: Ihre Tochter aber sahen sie nicht.
sentences.l: Their daughter, however, they did not see.
sentences.i: But their daughter they did not see.
sentences.n: The object is put first for contrast, which pushes the subject behind the verb — the V2 rule again.

sentences.t: Sie schauten das alles eine Zeitlang an, endlich faßten sie ein Herz und klopften leise ans Fenster.
sentences.l: They looked at all that for a while, at last they seized a heart and knocked softly at the window.
sentences.i: They watched all this for a while; at last they took heart and knocked softly at the window.
sentences.n: “ein Herz fassen” = to take heart, to pluck up courage. “ansehen” splits around the sentence: “schauten … an”.

sentences.t: Die Alte schien sie erwartet zu haben, sie stand auf und rief ganz freundlich „nur herein, ich kenne euch schon.“
sentences.l: The old woman seemed to have expected them, she stood up and called quite friendly “just come in, I know you already.”
sentences.i: The old woman seemed to have been expecting them; she got up and called out quite kindly: “Come in, I know you already.”
sentences.n: “nur herein” — “nur” with a command is encouraging: come along in. She knows without being told, as she has all through the tale.

sentences.t: Als sie in die Stube eingetreten waren, sprach die Alte „den weiten Weg hättet ihr euch sparen können, wenn ihr euer Kind, das so gut und liebreich ist, nicht vor drei Jahren ungerechter Weise verstoßen hättet.
sentences.l: When they had stepped into the parlour, the old woman spoke “the long way you could have spared yourselves, if you had not cast out your child, which is so good and loving, three years ago in an unjust manner.
sentences.i: When they had come into the room, the old woman said: “You might have spared yourselves the long journey, if you had not cast out your child — who is so good and loving — three years ago, and unjustly.
sentences.n: “ungerechter Weise” is written as two words in 1857 (modern ungerechterweise): in an unjust manner. The same spelling “weise” at the end of the tale is the adjective “wise”. “hättet … sparen können” is the unreal past: you could have spared.

sentences.t: Ihr hats nichts geschadet, sie hat drei Jahre lang die Gänse hüten müssen: sie hat nichts Böses dabei gelernt sondern ihr reines Herz behalten.
sentences.l: It has harmed her nothing, she has had to herd the geese three years long: she has learnt nothing bad at it but kept her pure heart.
sentences.i: It has done her no harm: she has had to herd geese for three years, and has learned nothing bad from it, but has kept her pure heart.
sentences.n: “schaden” takes the dative (“ihr”), and “hats” = hat es. The old woman’s verdict is the tale’s own: the service did the girl no harm.

sentences.t: Ihr aber seid durch die Angst, in der ihr gelebt habt, hinlänglich gestraft.“
sentences.l: You, however, are sufficiently punished by the fear in which you have lived.”
sentences.i: But you have been punished enough by the fear you have lived in.”
sentences.n: “hinlänglich” = sufficiently, amply. The relative clause keeps its preposition at the front (“in der ihr gelebt habt”), where English lets it slide to the end.

sentences.t: Dann gieng sie an die Kammer und rief „komm heraus, mein Töchterchen.“
sentences.l: Then she went to the chamber and called “come out, my little daughter.”
sentences.i: Then she went to the chamber door and called: “Come out, my little daughter.”
sentences.n: “herauskommen” is separable, particle heraus-: “komm heraus”.

sentences.t: Da gieng die Thüre auf, und die Königstochter trat heraus in ihrem seidenen Gewand mit ihren goldenen Haaren und ihren leuchtenden Augen, und es war als ob ein Engel vom Himmel käme.
sentences.l: Then the door went open, and the king’s daughter stepped out in her silken gown with her golden hair and her shining eyes, and it was as if an angel came from heaven.
sentences.i: Then the door opened, and the king’s daughter came out in her silk gown, with her golden hair and her shining eyes, and it was as though an angel had come from heaven.
sentences.n: “aufgehen” = to open, of a door (separable, particle auf-). “käme” is subjunctive after “als ob”.

sentences.t: Sie gieng auf ihren Vater und ihre Mutter zu, fiel ihnen um den Hals und küßte sie: es war nicht anders, sie mußten alle vor Freude weinen.
sentences.l: She went up to her father and her mother, fell them about the neck and kissed them: it was not otherwise, they all had to weep for joy.
sentences.i: She went up to her father and her mother, threw her arms about their necks and kissed them; there was no help for it — they all had to weep for joy.
sentences.n: “jemandem um den Hals fallen” = to fling one’s arms round someone’s neck, with the person in the dative. “es war nicht anders” = there was no help for it. “vor Freude” — “vor” gives the cause: for joy.

sentences.t: Der junge Graf stand neben ihnen, und als sie ihn erblickte, ward sie so roth im Gesicht wie eine Mosrose; sie wußte selbst nicht warum.
sentences.l: The young count stood beside them, and when she caught sight of him, she became so red in the face as a moss-rose; she did not know herself why.
sentences.i: The young count was standing beside them, and when she caught sight of him she turned as red as a moss-rose, and did not herself know why.
sentences.n: “Mosrose” is the 1857 spelling of Moosrose, the moss-rose. “ward” is the old past of werden. “selbst” here = herself, even she.

sentences.t: Der König sprach „liebes Kind, mein Königreich habe ich verschenkt, was soll ich dir geben?“
sentences.l: The king spoke “dear child, my kingdom I have given away, what shall I give you?”
sentences.i: The king said: “Dear child, I have given my kingdom away — what shall I give you?”
sentences.n: The object “mein Königreich” is fronted, which keeps the verb second and puts the subject after it. He has nothing left of what he divided at the beginning of his story.

sentences.t: „Sie braucht nichts,“ sagte die Alte, „ich schenke ihr die Thränen, die sie um euch geweint hat, das sind lauter Perlen, schöner als sie im Meer gefunden werden, und sind mehr werth als euer ganzes Königreich.
sentences.l: “She needs nothing,” said the old woman, “I give her the tears which she has wept for you, those are nothing but pearls, more beautiful than they are found in the sea, and are worth more than your whole kingdom.
sentences.i: “She needs nothing,” said the old woman; “I give her the tears she has wept for you. They are pearls and nothing else — finer than any found in the sea, and worth more than your whole kingdom.
sentences.n: “um euch geweint” = wept for you, over you. “werth” = wert. The gift is exactly what the king’s harshness produced: the tears themselves are the treasure.

sentences.t: Und zum Lohn für ihre Dienste gebe ich ihr mein Häuschen.“
sentences.l: And as wage for her services I give her my little house.”
sentences.i: And as payment for her services I give her my little house.”
sentences.n: “zum Lohn für” = as a reward for. What the little house is about to turn into is the tale’s last surprise.

sentences.t: Als die Alte das gesagt hatte, verschwand sie vor ihren Augen.
sentences.l: When the old woman had said that, she vanished before their eyes.
sentences.n: “vor ihren Augen” — before their eyes, in plain sight. Nothing explains her; the tale simply removes her.

sentences.t: Es knatterte ein wenig in den Wänden, und als sie sich umsahen, war das Häuschen in einen prächtigen Palast verwandelt, und eine königliche Tafel war gedeckt, und die Bedienten liefen hin und her.
sentences.l: It crackled a little in the walls, and when they looked round, the little house was transformed into a magnificent palace, and a royal table was laid, and the servants ran to and fro.
sentences.i: There was a slight crackling in the walls, and when they looked about them the little house had been changed into a splendid palace: a royal table was laid, and the attendants ran to and fro.
sentences.n: “knattern” = to crackle, to rattle. “sich umsehen” is separable, particle um-. “eine Tafel decken” = to lay a banquet table.

sentences.t: Die Geschichte geht noch weiter, aber meiner Großmutter, die sie mir erzählt hat, war das Gedächtnis schwach geworden: sie hatte das übrige vergessen.
sentences.l: The story goes still further, but to my grandmother, who told it to me, the memory had become weak: she had forgotten the rest.
sentences.i: The story goes on further still, but my grandmother, who told it to me, had grown weak in memory, and had forgotten the rest.
sentences.n: “meiner Großmutter … war das Gedächtnis schwach geworden” is a dative of possession — literally “to my grandmother the memory had grown weak”, i.e. her memory had failed. From here the storyteller speaks entirely in her own person.

sentences.t: Ich glaube immer die schöne Königstochter ist mit dem Grafen vermählt worden, und sie sind zusammen in dem Schloß geblieben und haben da in aller Glückseligkeit gelebt so lange Gott wollte.
sentences.l: I always believe the beautiful king’s daughter has been married to the count, and they have stayed together in the castle and have lived there in all blessedness as long as God willed.
sentences.i: I have always believed that the fair king’s daughter was married to the count, and that they stayed together in the castle and lived there in all happiness as long as God willed.
sentences.n: “ich glaube immer” = I keep thinking, I have always thought — she offers it as her own guess, not as the tale. “so lange Gott wollte” is an old closing formula that stops short of promising for ever.

sentences.t: Ob die schneeweißen Gänse, die bei dem Häuschen gehütet wurden, lauter Mädchen waren (es brauchts niemand übel zu nehmen), welche die Alte zu sich genommen hatte,
sentences.l: Whether the snow-white geese which were herded at the little house were nothing but girls (nobody need take it amiss), whom the old woman had taken to herself,
sentences.i: Whether the snow-white geese that were tended at the little house were all of them girls (let nobody take offence at that), whom the old woman had taken in,
sentences.n: The round brackets are the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text — not an editorial addition here. “übel nehmen” = to take amiss, and “brauchts” = braucht es: nobody need take it amiss. The clause breaks off unfinished and is picked up in the next unit.

sentences.t: und ob sie jetzt ihre menschliche Gestalt wieder erhielten, und als Dienerinnen bei der jungen Königin blieben, das weiß ich nicht genau, aber ich vermuthe es doch.
sentences.l: and whether they now received their human shape again, and stayed as serving-women with the young queen, that I do not know exactly, but I do suppose it.
sentences.i: and whether they now got their human shape back and stayed on as waiting-women to the young queen — that I do not know for certain, but I suppose they did.
sentences.n: “das weiß ich nicht genau” — the fronted “das” gathers up both long “ob” clauses. “vermuthe” = vermute, I suppose. “Dienerinnen” is the feminine plural of Diener.

sentences.t: So viel ist gewiß, daß die Alte keine Hexe war, wie die Leute glaubten, sondern eine weise Frau, die es gut meinte.
sentences.l: So much is certain, that the old woman was no witch, as the people believed, but a wise woman who meant it well.
sentences.i: So much is certain: the old woman was no witch, as people believed, but a wise woman who meant well.
sentences.n: “weise” here is the adjective, wise — a “weise Frau” is a cunning woman, a healer and helper, the opposite of what the village said of her. The same spelling meant “manner” a few lines earlier, in “ungerechter Weise”.

sentences.t: Wahrscheinlich ist sie es auch gewesen, die der Königstochter schon bei der Geburt die Gabe verliehen hat Perlen zu weinen statt der Thränen.
sentences.l: Probably it was also she who granted to the king’s daughter, already at her birth, the gift of weeping pearls instead of tears.
sentences.i: Most likely it was she, too, who at the king’s daughter’s birth granted her the gift of weeping pearls instead of tears.
sentences.n: “verleihen” = to bestow, to confer, as of a gift or a title. “statt” takes the genitive: “statt der Thränen”.

sentences.t: Heutzutage kommt das nicht mehr vor, sonst könnten die Armen bald reich werden.
sentences.l: Nowadays that no longer comes about, otherwise the poor could soon become rich.
sentences.i: Nowadays such things no longer happen, or the poor might soon be rich.
sentences.n: “vorkommen” = to occur, to happen (separable, particle vor-). The last line is the storyteller’s dry aside on her own tale.

glossary.ausgezogen: ausziehen — set out, gone forth (past part.; separable, particle aus-)
glossary.ausziehe: ausziehen — I move out, I leave the house (1st sg.; separable, particle aus-)
glossary.besorgt: besorgt — anxious, afraid (adjective; er war besorgt = he was afraid)
glossary.denk: denken — think (imperative sg.; denk dir = just imagine — plain High German here, not Low German)
glossary.fuhr: fortfahren — went on, continued speaking (3rd sg. past; separable, particle fort-: fuhr … fort)
glossary.gebeten: bitten — begged, entreated (past part.; für sie gefleht und gebeten = pleaded and begged for her)
glossary.gekostet: kosten — cost (past part.; das Leben gekostet = cost one’s life)
glossary.halt: aufhalten — hold up, delay (imperative sg.; separable, particle auf-: halt … auf)
glossary.herde: die Herde — herd, flock (not der Herd, a hearth)
glossary.hielt: halten — held; halten für = to take for, to consider (3rd sg. past)
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, told, ordered (3rd sg. past, with a bare infinitive); also “was called”
glossary.jünglinge: der Jüngling — youth, young man (dat. sg. with the old -e ending)
glossary.langte: anlangen — arrived (3rd sg. past; separable, particle an-: langte … an)
glossary.ließen: lassen — let, allowed (3rd pl. past; hören lassen = to let be heard, to utter)
glossary.lust: die Lust — delight, high spirits; Lust haben = to have a mind to do something
glossary.müßt: müssen — must (2nd pl. present; 1857 spelling of müsst)
glossary.obst: das Obst — fruit (collective; das wilde Obst = the wild fruit — plain High German here)
glossary.rede: reden — speak (imperative sg.; rede kein Wort weiter = speak not another word)
glossary.rühren: rühren — to move, to stir (das Herz rühren = to touch the heart)
glossary.sage: sagen — I say (1st sg.; ich sage dir = I tell you — not die Sage, a legend)
glossary.sagt: sagen — say, tell (imperative pl.: sagt mir = tell me; also 3rd sg. sagt, says)
glossary.schau: schauen — look (imperative sg.; sich umschauen = to look round, separable, particle um-)
glossary.schickt: schicken — send (imperative pl.: schickt mich nicht fort = do not send me away); in ‘es schickt sich nicht’ the verb is sich schicken, to be fitting
glossary.sei: sein — be (imperative sg.: sei ohne Sorgen); also subjunctive I of reported speech: sie sei = she is (as reported)
glossary.sollt: sollen — you are to, you shall (2nd pl.; ihr sollt mir sagen = you are to tell me)
glossary.sonst: sonst — else; otherwise (was sonst = what else; sonst könnten … = otherwise they could …)
glossary.stellt: sich vorstellen — imagine (imperative pl.; separable, particle vor-: stellt euch vor)
glossary.streckten: strecken — stretched, put out (3rd pl. past; streckten die Flügel in die Höhe = stretched their wings up)
glossary.strich: streichen — brushed, swept (3rd sg. past; of a breeze moving through leaves)
glossary.tröste: sich trösten — I comfort myself (1st sg.; ich tröste mich mit der Hoffnung = I comfort myself with the hope)
glossary.vorstellen: sich vorstellen — to imagine, to picture to oneself (separable, particle vor-)
glossary.wann: wann — when (in an indirect question: ich weiß nicht wann = I do not know when)
glossary.weise: weise — wise (adjective); also die Weise — way, manner
glossary.weiß: weiß — white (adjective); also wissen — know (1st/3rd sg.: ich weiß, wer weiß)
glossary.wenden: sich wenden — to turn, to turn to (wohin ich mich wenden kann = where I can turn)
glossary.werde: werden — I shall (1st sg. present, as future auxiliary: daran werde ich es sehen)
glossary.wozu: wozu — for what, to what end
glossary.wulle: wulle — the geese’s cry, and the call used to bring geese in (High German; not the Low German form of wollte)
glossary.zieh: anziehen — put on (imperative sg.; separable, particle an-: zieh … an)
glossary.ächzen: das Ächzen — groaning (verbal noun; unter beständigem Ächzen = with constant groaning)
